wokeTrap.explanation: Captain America: Brave New World is not a woke trap. Unlike Conclave, which disguised its ideology inside prestige packaging, this film's content is exactly what the marketing promised: a Black Captain America, a storyline about government experimentation on Black soldiers, and a plot that pits Sam Wilson against a system that wronged people who look like him. The ideological content is visible from the trailer. No deception here. What you see is what you get.

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Not a woke trap. The film's racial themes, the Isaiah Bradley subplot (government experimentation on a Black super soldier), and the elevation of 'empathy as superpower' are visible from the marketing. Conservative viewers are not being ambushed. The film wears its ideology openly. The question is not whether it's deceptive but whether the ideology is central enough to damage the film. Our scoring says: it's noticeable but not overwhelming.

director.name: Julius Onah
director.ideology: Progressive. Nigerian-American filmmaker who has spoken openly about using superhero cinema to explore themes of race, empathy, and systemic injustice. Described Sam Wilson's 'superpower' as empathy. Not a provocateur but a true believer.
director.profile: Nigerian-American director (b. 1983). Previously directed The Cloverfield Paradox (2018), which received poor reviews. Brave New World is his biggest studio assignment. Onah has spoken publicly about wanting to use Sam Wilson's Captain America to explore racial identity and institutional trust. He stated empathy was Wilson's 'superpower' and wanted to use the character's 'emotional intelligence' to resolve the film's conflicts. This is a director who believes the superhero genre is a vehicle for social messaging.

writer.name: Rob Edwards, Malcolm Spellman & Dalan Musson, Julius Onah & Peter Glanz
writer.profile: Multiple writers with screenplay-by-committee issues. Malcolm Spellman created The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, which featured extended commentary on race in America, the Tuskegee experiment parallels with Isaiah Bradley, and explicit dialogue about what it means for a Black man to carry Captain America's shield. Rob Edwards (The Princess and the Frog) and Peter Glanz were brought in during extensive reshoots. The writing team's ideological orientation is progressive across the board.

top_cast.name: Anthony Mackie
top_cast.notes: Mackie has been outspoken about the political dimensions of playing a Black Captain America. In a Rome press conference, he said the character represents 'everybody' and then had to clarify comments after online backlash from fans who felt he was distancing from the racial significance. He described his performance as inspired by Tupac's 'Hit Em Up.' Progressive casting by definition: Sam Wilson replaces Steve Rogers as Captain America.

top_cast.name: Harrison Ford
top_cast.notes: Ford replaces the late William Hurt, who played Ross in The Incredible Hulk (2008). His Ross becomes president, is secretly dying, and transforms into Red Hulk after being dosed with gamma radiation by the villain. The spectacle of a president destroying the White House from the podium drew obvious political comparisons.

top_cast.name: Carl Lumbly
top_cast.notes: Reprising his role from The Falcon and the Winter Soldier. Isaiah is a Black Korean War veteran and super soldier who was imprisoned and experimented on by the U.S. government for 30 years. The character is explicitly inspired by the Tuskegee Syphilis Study. His presence is the film's most direct injection of racial politics.

celebrity_mentions.name: Anthony Mackie
celebrity_mentions.context: Made controversial comments at a Rome press conference about what Captain America represents, sparking backlash from both progressive and conservative audiences.

celebrity_mentions.name: Ben Shapiro

summary.overall:
Captain America: Brave New World is the most politically charged Marvel film since Black Panther, and it arrives at the worst possible moment for a studio that just wants to sell tickets without starting a culture war.

Anthony Mackie's Sam Wilson officially takes over the shield from Chris Evans' Steve Rogers, making him the first Black Captain America in the MCU. Harrison Ford joins as President Thaddeus Ross, who secretly transforms into Red Hulk. The film grossed $415 million worldwide on a $180 million budget. Critics were mixed (52% on Rotten Tomatoes), audiences warmer (78%). It is the definition of a middling blockbuster: competently assembled, narratively overstuffed, and ideologically loaded enough to guarantee controversy without being bold enough to earn it.

Let's dig in.

> SPOILER ALERT: This review discusses the full plot in detail.

---

## The Plot

Five months after Thaddeus Ross (Harrison Ford) wins the presidency, he sends Sam Wilson and his partner Joaquin Torres, the new Falcon (Danny Ramirez), to Oaxaca, Mexico to stop the sale of stolen classified items by the mercenary group Serpent Society. They recover the items but the leader escapes.

Back in D.C., Ross invites Wilson to a White House summit with world leaders. The central issue: a new metal called adamantium has been discovered on 'Celestial Island,' formed when the Celestial Tiamut emerged from the Indian Ocean. Ross proposes an international treaty to govern its mining. During the summit, the song 'Mr. Blue' plays and several attendees, including Isaiah Bradley (Carl Lumbly), a Black super soldier who was imprisoned and experimented on by the U.S. government for 30 years, are mind-controlled into shooting at Ross and other dignitaries.

Wilson investigates and discovers the mastermind is Dr. Samuel Sterns (Tim Blake Nelson), the 'Leader,' who gained super-intelligence from exposure to Hulk blood and was imprisoned by Ross at a secret black site called Camp Echo One. Ross had promised to release Sterns in exchange for pills that extended Ross's life, which were dying of heart failure. When Ross reneged, Sterns plotted revenge.

The climax unfolds on Celestial Island where American and Japanese forces race to claim the adamantium. Sterns triggers a crisis that nearly starts an international conflict. Torres is critically injured. Ross, at a press conference where his connection to Sterns is exposed, loses control and transforms into Red Hulk, destroying part of the White House.

Wilson talks Ross down by reminding him of visiting D.C.'s cherry blossom trees with his estranged daughter Betty (Liv Tyler). Ross reverts to human form. Aftermath: Bradley is exonerated, Torres is invited to join the Avengers, the treaty is ratified, and Ross resigns and voluntarily incarcerates himself at the Raft.

---

## The Ideological Content

This is not a radical film. But it's not a neutral one, either.

**1. The Isaiah Bradley Subplot: America's Racial Sins as Plot Engine.** Isaiah Bradley is a character explicitly modeled on the victims of the Tuskegee Syphilis Study, in which the U.S. government conducted unethical medical experiments on Black men. In The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, Isaiah told Sam that America would never accept a Black Captain America. In this film, he is framed for an assassination attempt through mind control, putting a wrongfully imprisoned Black veteran in the crosshairs once again. His exoneration at the end is presented as a moral victory. The racial politics are clear: America's institutions have betrayed Black men, and Sam Wilson's Captain America exists to right those wrongs. This is not subtext. It is text.

**2. Empathy as Superpower.** Director Julius Onah has stated repeatedly that empathy is Sam Wilson's defining trait. Unlike Steve Rogers, who was a super soldier first and a leader second, Wilson wins through 'listening, compassion, and counseling,' in Mackie's words. The film's climax is not a fight scene. It is Sam talking the Red Hulk down from a rage by appealing to his relationship with his daughter. This is a deliberate philosophical statement: the new Captain America wins not through strength but through emotional intelligence. Some conservative viewers will find this refreshing. Others will find it a direct import of therapeutic culture into a franchise built on punching Nazis.

**3. The Conspiracy Plot: Government as Villain.** The film's central conspiracy involves a U.S. president who secretly imprisoned a man, broke his promise, and was sustained by pills that were slowly turning him into a monster. The government is not the good guys here. This is not inherently progressive. Anti-government conspiracy has a long history on the American right. But combined with the Isaiah Bradley subplot, the message becomes specifically about how American institutions have targeted Black men. That narrows the critique from 'distrust government' (which conservatives agree with) to 'distrust government because of racial injustice' (which frames the conversation in progressive terms).

**4. Sam Wilson as 'Non-Judgmental' Captain America.** Mackie said Wilson 'has a different understanding of good and evil' than Rogers and would not be a 'judgmental' Captain America. This is therapeutic language applied to a moral role. Steve Rogers punched Nazis and told people to stand for something. Sam Wilson's Captain America is framed as someone who listens first and judges never. Whether you find this an evolution or a dilution depends on your worldview.

## Creative Team Deep Dive

### Full Cast

| Actor | Role |
|---|---|
| Anthony Mackie | Sam Wilson / Captain America |
| Danny Ramirez | Joaquin Torres / Falcon |

| Carl Lumbly | Isaiah Bradley |

| Harrison Ford | President Thaddeus Ross / Red Hulk |

### Director: Julius Onah

**The Cloverfield Paradox (2018):** Sci-fi thriller released directly to Netflix after Paramount sold it. Poorly received (16% on Rotten Tomatoes). No significant ideological content.

**Captain America: Brave New World (2025):** His first major studio film. Onah has been transparent about his goals: use the Captain America franchise to explore racial identity, empathy, and the relationship between Black Americans and the institutions that have betrayed them. He said Wilson has to 'see past his own blind spots' regarding Ross, language that imports therapeutic culture into the superhero genre. Onah is not a subtle filmmaker, but he's earnest.

### Writers: Malcolm Spellman & Dalan Musson

Spellman created The Falcon and the Winter Soldier (2021), the Disney+ series that set up Wilson's Captain America. That series featured extensive commentary on race in America, including the Isaiah Bradley backstory, explicit parallels to the Tuskegee experiments, and a monologue by Sam Wilson about what it means to be a Black man carrying America's shield. Spellman is the ideological architect of this version of Captain America.

### Producers: Kevin Feige / Marvel Studios

Feige has overseen the MCU since its inception. Under his leadership, Marvel has moved steadily toward more diverse representation (Black Panther, Shang-Chi, Ms. Marvel, Captain America: Brave New World). Feige does not make ideological films. He makes commercially calculated films that incorporate just enough progressive representation to satisfy Disney's stakeholder commitments without alienating the broad audience. This is corporate progressivism: profitable, calibrated, and never truly radical.

### Composer: Laura Karpman

Karpman scored the film. She is the first woman to compose the music for a Captain America film. Her previous credits include The Marvels (2023) and Lovecraft Country (2020), the latter of which explored racial horror in 1950s America. Her work on Brave New World is competent but unremarkable.

### Fidelity Casting Analysis

**Sam Wilson as Captain America:** In the comics, Sam Wilson has been Captain America since 2014, and the transition was a major event. In the MCU, the handoff from Rogers to Wilson was established in Avengers: Endgame (2019) and The Falcon and the Winter Soldier (2021). This is not a diversity swap. It is a faithful adaptation of existing Marvel Comics continuity. **Fidelity Score: High.**

**Thaddeus Ross (Harrison Ford):** Ford replaces William Hurt, who died in 2022. The recasting is respectful and narratively justified. Ross's transformation to Red Hulk follows comic book canon. **Fidelity Score: High.**

**Isaiah Bradley (Carl Lumbly):** Based on the 2003 comic series Truth: Red, White & Black, which depicted Black soldiers experimented on by the U.S. government. The character is faithful to source material. **Fidelity Score: High.**

---

## Adult Viewer Insight

Captain America: Brave New World is not the ideological grenade some conservative commentators feared. It is not Black Panther-level identity politics. It is not an anti-white screed. It is a mediocre Marvel movie with real but moderate progressive content.

The Isaiah Bradley subplot is the most ideologically loaded element. It directly invokes the Tuskegee experiments and frames the U.S. government as an institution that systematically betrayed Black Americans. This is historical fact, but the film uses it as a moral framework for the entire story. If that framework bothers you, the film will bother you.

The 'empathy as superpower' angle is softer but still noticeable. Steve Rogers was a leader who stood for things. Sam Wilson is framed as a leader who listens. Whether that's an upgrade or a downgrade depends on what you think Captain America should represent.

The positive elements are real. Personal responsibility matters: Ross accepts his punishment. Military service is honored. The father-daughter bond is the emotional climax. Patriotism, defined as 'defending America while acknowledging its failures,' is the film's framework. You may disagree with the emphasis on failures, but the patriotism is genuine.

Bottom line: watchable, not inflammatory, ideologically moderate-left. You'll survive it.

---

## Parental Guidance

**Rated PG-13** for intense sequences of violence and action, and some strong language.

- **Violence:** Significant. Superhero action violence throughout, including gunfire, explosions, hand-to-hand combat, and the Red Hulk transformation destroying parts of the White House. A character is killed on screen. Torres is critically injured.
- **Sexual Content:** None.
- **Language:** Some strong language, mild by Marvel standards.
- **Substance Use:** None significant.
- **Themes:** Government conspiracy, racial injustice, betrayal of trust, mind control, terminal illness.
- **Specific Concern for Conservative Families:** The Isaiah Bradley subplot explicitly parallels the Tuskegee Syphilis Study and frames U.S. institutions as having systematically betrayed Black Americans. Younger viewers may absorb this framing without historical context. Parents should be prepared to discuss the difference between acknowledging historical injustice (appropriate) and using it as a lens to view all American institutions as inherently racist (ideological).

**Age recommendation:** 10+ for action content, with parental context for the racial themes.

tropeAudit.name: Black Captain America as racial reckoning narrative
tropeAudit.description: Sam Wilson's Captain America is not just a new hero. He is specifically framed as a Black man carrying a historically white symbol, and the film makes this racial dimension explicit. The Falcon and the Winter Soldier established that Wilson must 'earn' the shield in a country that has never accepted a Black Captain America. This film continues that framing. The racial commentary is integral to Wilson's character and informs every major relationship. Authenticity is moderate because Sam Wilson has been Captain America in the comics since 2014; this is not a pure diversity invention, but the MCU amplifies the racial dimension beyond the source material.

tropeAudit.name: Isaiah Bradley: Tuskegee parallel and government experimentation on Black soldiers
tropeAudit.description: Isaiah Bradley is a Black super soldier who was imprisoned and experimented on by the U.S. government for 30 years. The character is explicitly inspired by the real Tuskegee Syphilis Study. In this film, he is framed for an assassination attempt through mind control, putting a wrongfully imprisoned Black veteran in danger once again. His exoneration at the end is presented as a moral triumph. The ideological function is to keep America's racial sins at the center of the franchise's moral universe. Authenticity is moderate because the character comes directly from the 2003 comics.

tropeAudit.name: 'Empathy as superpower' replaces traditional masculine heroism
tropeAudit.description: Director Onah stated Wilson's 'superpower' is empathy. Mackie described Wilson as 'non-judgmental' with a 'different understanding of good and evil.' The climax is not a fight but a conversation: Wilson talks the Red Hulk down by invoking his relationship with his daughter. This replaces the physical, decisive, morally certain heroism of Steve Rogers with a therapeutic model of leadership: listening, understanding, and refusing to judge. It is a deliberate philosophical shift that maps onto the progressive preference for emotional intelligence over moral clarity.

tropeAudit.name: Government conspiracy framed through racial injustice lens
tropeAudit.description: The film's conspiracy plot involves a president who secretly imprisoned a man and broke his word. Anti-government conspiracy is not inherently progressive. But the specific combination with the Isaiah Bradley subplot frames institutional distrust specifically through the lens of racial injustice rather than general government overreach. This narrows the critique from 'distrust the state' (broad) to 'distrust the state because it's racist' (progressive).

tropeAudit.name: Non-judgmental Captain America with 'different understanding of good and evil'
tropeAudit.description: Mackie described his Captain America as someone who wouldn't be judgmental and has a 'different understanding of good and evil' than Rogers. This is therapeutic relativism applied to a character who historically represents moral certainty. Rogers told people to stand up for what's right. Wilson's version is framed as someone who understands that right and wrong are more complicated. Low authenticity because the comics' Sam Wilson was not morally ambiguous; this framing is a film-specific invention.

tropeAudit.name: DEI-adjacent casting discourse baked into marketing
tropeAudit.description: The film's release during Trump's second term, following anti-DEI executive orders, guaranteed that Sam Wilson's promotion to Captain America would be labeled a 'DEI move' by conservative commentators. While this is partly external to the film, the marketing leaned into the racial significance rather than away from it. The Hollywood Reporter noted the film 'sparked another Disney culture war.'

tropeAudit.name: Israeli character presented uncritically as hero
tropeAudit.description: Ruth Bat-Seraph (Shira Haas) is an Israeli former Black Widow who serves as Ross's head of security and becomes an ally to Wilson. Her Israeli identity is not politicized in the film. This is a minor note, scored low, but worth flagging given the broader Disney context and the Israel-Palestine culture war dynamics.

tropeAudit.name: Strong female supporting character with combat skills equal to male heroes
tropeAudit.description: Bat-Seraph fights alongside Wilson and Torres as a combat equal. This is standard MCU practice and faithful to the Black Widow tradition. Scored low because it's genre-standard and doesn't feel forced.

tropeAudit.name: Villain's plan uses mind control specifically on Black man
tropeAudit.description: Samuel Sterns specifically mind-controls Isaiah Bradley into shooting at the president, framing a Black man who was already victimized by the government. The choice to use Bradley as the mind-controlled patsy doubles down on the racial injustice theme: even after 30 years of imprisonment, America's system finds ways to weaponize Black men.

tropeAudit.name: Personal responsibility: Ross accepts consequences and voluntarily incarcerates himself
tropeAudit.description: After his transformation and the destruction he causes, President Ross does not make excuses. He resigns and voluntarily incarcerates himself at the Raft. This is a straightforward affirmation of personal accountability: when you cause harm, you face the consequences, even if you're the president. This is one of the film's strongest traditional moral notes.

tropeAudit.name: Mentorship and earned authority (Wilson mentors Torres)
tropeAudit.description: Wilson takes Torres under his wing (literally), mentoring him into the Falcon role. This echoes the Rogers-Wilson dynamic and affirms the traditional value of mentorship: authority is earned through competence and service, then passed to the next generation. Wilson is initially protective of Torres, wanting to shield him from danger. It's a solid traditional relationship.

tropeAudit.name: Patriotism: Captain America defends America despite its flaws
tropeAudit.description: For all the racial commentary, Sam Wilson still wears the stars and stripes. He still calls himself Captain America. He still defends the country and its institutions, even the ones that wronged men like Isaiah Bradley. The film's version of patriotism is 'love the country enough to make it better,' which is more progressive than Rogers' straightforward patriotism but is still genuinely patriotic. Wilson never renounces America. He fights for it.

tropeAudit.name: Father-daughter bond as emotional anchor
tropeAudit.description: The climax turns on Ross's relationship with his estranged daughter Betty (Liv Tyler). Wilson talks Ross down from his Red Hulk rage by reminding him of cherry blossom walks with Betty. The father-daughter bond is presented as the most powerful force in the film, stronger than gamma radiation or political power. This is a strong traditional element.

tropeAudit.name: Military service honored
tropeAudit.description: Wilson is a former Air Force pararescueman. Torres is a first lieutenant. Their military backgrounds are treated with respect and inform their competence. Military service is not satirized or questioned. It is the foundation of their capability.

tropeAudit.name: Corruption exposed and punished
tropeAudit.description: Samuel Sterns is captured and imprisoned. Ross's secret dealings are exposed and he faces consequences. The film affirms that corruption, even at the highest levels of government, should be exposed and punished. No one is above accountability.

tropeAudit.name: International cooperation through treaty and diplomacy over war
tropeAudit.description: The adamantium treaty is ratified. The U.S. and Japan avoid armed conflict. Diplomacy prevails. While international cooperation is not exclusively a conservative value, the emphasis on preventing unnecessary war and resolving disputes through agreements is consistent with traditional statecraft.

tropeAudit.name: Self-sacrifice: Torres critically injured protecting others
tropeAudit.description: Joaquin Torres is critically injured in the fight to prevent a military confrontation, protecting others at great personal cost. Self-sacrifice in service of others is a core traditional hero value and is treated with appropriate weight in the film.
